opt:body.p: A time-series chart that follows a film's clock. It draws the sampled series of a recorded interaction with a playhead, a played bar and a chapter bar, and it moves only when the film it is bound to says so: the film broadcasts opt-film-time on every tick, and the chart reads the time from it. It is a projection of the film's timeline, like the machine diagram, not a second player.

Every page that carries a chart ships it pre-rendered. The build lowers the data block into a declarative shadow root with the finished SVG, a caption with a one-paragraph summary and the data as a real table behind a disclosure, so the chart is complete before any script runs and stays complete where WebAssembly is unavailable, as it is in Firefox on ppc64le. When the element upgrades it keeps that markup if the data block still matches the hash the build embedded, and keeps the pre-rendered chart itself when its width already fits the container; otherwise it lays the chart out at the measured width. From then on a resize observer re-lays it out whenever the container changes, so text stays its token size, and below 480 px every second tick label goes, and the chapter bar with the buttons on its cues, so a chapter that is not drawn is not reachable either.

Series take their colour from the palette tokens (--op-series-1 to 6) by position, and colour is never the only cue: each series after the first has its own dash pattern, a labelled series ends in a direct label with a swatch, an unlabelled one carries markers, and the forced-colours, high-contrast and print rules are the film's.

opt:film.title: Eight frames of a theme flight

opt:body.p: One script child of type application/json holds the data. The build reads it to pre-render the chart and embeds a hash of it on the element; the upgraded element reads the same block, so authors write one thing.

tr.td: The length of the timeline; required, positive.
One entry per column after time: id and label, an optional unit, and optional dash and marker indices that override the cues chosen by position.
Each row is [t, v1, ..., vN] with one value per series, in non-decreasing time; null marks a missing sample and breaks the line.
Optional { "t", "title" } entries drawn on the chapter bar.
Optional value domain; when absent, series measured in % whose values fit the film's percent scale take it, and anything else the range of the data padded by four percent on each side.

opt:body.p: The block may not contain the character sequence that closes a script element; the build escapes it inside strings, and the parser rejects anything outside this schema naming the offending key.

Every gesture and key on the chart asks the film for a time; the chart never moves its own playhead. It sends opt-chart-seek to commit, opt-chart-peek to preview and opt-chart-toggle to play or pause, and the film applies them to its clock and broadcasts the result, which is what the chart draws. A chart bound to another film is ignored, so several charts can share a page.

Where the pointer can hover and is a precise one, hovering the plot previews the sample nearest it, or the time under it where no sample is within 40 pixels: the peek rule and its readout follow the pointer, the chart takes the peeking state, and the film's clock does not move. A press that does not travel more than three pixels is a tap, and it seeks where it lands when released. A press that travels further becomes a pending seek: the chart takes the pending state, the preview shows where the release would land, and the release commits it. Escape abandons a pending seek and leaves the clock where it was. With a coarse pointer there is no hover, and a press held for half a second starts the same pending seek.
opt:body.opt:callout: Bringing the pointer back within four pixels of where the press began says the seek will be abandoned: the chart takes the cancelling state while the pointer stays there, aiming away again resumes the seek, and releasing inside that band abandons it. The research this element is built on rates the gesture as an extrapolation from a mobile-only pattern, so it ships to be judged in use and may be withdrawn.
opt:body.p: Tabbing reaches the playhead, which is the slider that announces the time, and the data table's disclosure after it. Keys act only while the chart has focus, and each one asks for a time rather than moving the playhead itself. While a mark or a chapter has the focus the arrows step between them rather than along the timeline. A seek from the chart pauses the film, as the film's own seeks do, and the same keys are named in a line under every chart, beside the summary of what it holds.
